opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was a mix of curiosity and skepticism. Aravind and I come from a similar research background, so I knew him as someone very sharp and very ambitious. But when he showed me that early demo, it was still pretty rough. You'd type in a question, it would pull some search results, and a language model would summarize them with citations. Technically, none of the individual pieces felt like a breakthrough. It was more of a clever combination.

And then he started talking about going after Google. I remember thinking, okay, that's a very bold thing to say. Google is probably the most entrenched product on the internet, with an enormous infrastructure, a huge talent pool, and decades of search expertise. As a researcher, my instinct was, "Where's the moat? Couldn't Google just do this themselves in six months?"

But what I underestimated was that the hard part wasn't just the model. It was the product sense, the speed, and the willingness to bet everything on a new interaction paradigm. Aravind saw very early that people didn't really want ten blue links; they wanted an answer they could trust, with sources. Big companies have a lot to lose by changing that experience, especially when their business model depends on ads around those links. A startup doesn't have that baggage.

So looking back, I'd say my reaction was respectful doubt. I thought the idea was interesting but maybe too ambitious. Over time I came to appreciate that in this era, conviction and execution can matter as much as any single technical innovation. That was a good lesson for me as someone who mostly lives in the research world.

r001.rationale: The response describes the demo as a rough combination of search results and a language model, but it never says Xie privately questioned whether it was merely a wrapper around GPT.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was a bit of skepticism, mixed with admiration for the ambition. Aravind and I overlapped in the research world, and when he showed me that early demo, it was very raw. It was basically a language model wrapped around a search index, with citations. And my instinct as a researcher was to poke at it: what happens when the model hallucinates, how do you handle freshness, what's the business model when Google has a 20-year head start and essentially infinite compute.

But what struck me was that he wasn't framing it as "we'll build a better ranking algorithm." He was framing it as a different interface to knowledge. You ask a question, you get an answer with sources, not ten blue links. And once I used it for a few days for my own literature searches, I realized the experience was actually different in a way that was hard to go back from. It changed my mental model of what a search product could be.

I also think there's something about the timing. Many of us in academia saw the capabilities of these models but didn't have the appetite to bet a company on them. Aravind did. Whether or not you revolutionize Google, taking that swing when the technology is just barely good enough is where the interesting outcomes come from. So I went from "this is a cool demo" to "okay, this might actually matter" fairly quickly.

r001.rationale: The response describes the demo as a language model wrapped around a search index, but does not identify GPT or say Xie privately questioned whether the demo was merely a GPT wrapper.

sol-6.1.text: My first reaction was skepticism. Google is such a strong product, so when someone says they’re going to reinvent search, you naturally wonder how. But the demo made the idea much more concrete: instead of giving you links and leaving you to piece things together, it could give you an answer directly. I could see why that might change how people search. That’s different from knowing whether it could beat Google, but it was enough to take the ambition seriously.
